extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature and drama; literary critics and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical analysis of Persian passion-plays (tazya) and related literary pieces: what theatrical, thematic, and cultural elements produce their intense emotional effect; also evaluation of the writer Joseph Joubert as an example of an 'obscure genius.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and communal production for catastrophic scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: For this catastrophe no one tazya suffices; all the companies of actors unite in a vast open space; booths and tents are pitched round the outside circle for the spectators; in the centre is the Imam's camp, and the day ends with its conflagration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dramatization of Kerbela's final catastrophe requires a large-scale, communal staging (multiple companies, open arena, surrounding booths/tents) culminating in a spectacular ending (conflagration). The magnitude of the event on stage must match the narrative magnitude to produce the intended public emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of aftermath tableau to produce extraordinary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces which carry on the story beyond the death of Hussein — e.g., The Christian Damsel — show the silent plain of Kerbela and the tombs of the martyrs; bodies full of wounds with weapons sticking in them are exposed, but surrounded by crowns of burning candles to show they have entered into glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct post-battle tableaux that juxtapose physical horror (wounded corpses) with symbolic markers of sanctity (crowns of candles, tombs) to deepen poignancy and produce a striking audience response. Detailed visual composition is central to effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic physical detail and visceral spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes expose bodies full of wounds, weapons sticking in them, blood springing up wherever a pole is driven into the ground; physical ill-treatment of corpses produces horror in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, corporeal detail (wounds, blood, mutilation) as a deliberate device to elicit horror and pity. Such visceral elements are a key mechanism for raising audience emotion in these plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural apparitions and canonical figures to reveal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus Christ, angels, prophets, Mahomet, Moses, the Imams, and holy women appear on the sakou to explain or sanctify events (e.g., Jesus reveals Kerbela to the sleeping damsel; Hussein's voice calls out from his tomb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appearances of religious/supernatural figures and voice-from-the-tomb devices to interpret the scene for the audience, confer spiritual significance, and facilitate conversions or revelations within the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic visual motifs (candles, doves, tombs, caravans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowns of burning candles and circles of light show martyrs have entered into glory; white doves hover over Hussein; a brilliant caravan enters with exotic costume to create spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate recurring visual symbols (light/candles for sanctity, doves for purity, tombs as focal points, caravans as exotic spectacle) to convey thematic meaning non-verbally and amplify emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional focus on family, women, and children to heighten pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The Family of the Tent is full of women and children, whose devotion and sufferings — blameless women and lovely innocent children (e.g., Sekyna, four years old, taking Hussein's head and dying in a vision of happiness) — supply tender pathos that augments the central martyr's sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: foreground family suffering (especially women and children) and intimate scenes of loss to magnify sympathy and create a tender, overpowering ideal of self-sacrifice in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotism and ethnic identification as a source of popular emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Count Gobineau suggests that Persians identify Hussein with Persia — 'Hussein ... represent the nation, represent Persia, invaded, ill-treated, despoiled' — so patriotic feeling combines with religious mourning to intensify response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and, if appropriate, leverage collective identification (national/ethnic grievances) in the subject-matter so that martyrdom functions as a portrait of communal suffering and gains additional emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/character virtues as engines of sympathy (abnegation, mildness, self-sacrifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abnegation and mildness, based on the depth of the inner life and visited by unmerited misfortune, made the power of the Imams over the popular imagination. These saintly self-deniers supplied a tender and pathetic side in Islam that attracts sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray central figures with inwardness, gentleness, and resigned self-sacrifice to create a moral exemplar whose suffering invites deep compassion. The contrast between moral purity and worldly injustice intensifies audience devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious‑comparative framing to explain universal appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay argues Christianity supplies 'mildness and sweet reasonableness' (a power of presenting duty as intuition) that the Imams lack; yet the Imams' mildness and self-sacrifice still point toward the same human need — suggesting why the drama's emotional content has wide appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative cultural/religious framing in criticism or composition to situate the play's virtues relative to other traditions; this can explain why certain motifs resonate cross-culturally and highlight which emotional qualities are missing or present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging for interactive audience reaction and ritualistic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Booths and tents are pitched for spectators around the outside circle; groans and audible horror arise from the audience at particular moments (e.g., blood springing up when poles are driven).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design performance spaces and moments that invite collective, audible reactions from the audience (gasps, groans, shouts) and incorporate ritual elements that make the spectator part of the event rather than a passive observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conversion/narrative arc (e.g., foreign witness becomes believer)
rubrics_metrics.description: In The Christian Damsel, a European‑costumed lady wakes after a vision, embraces Islam, and narratively affirms the moral/spiritual truth revealed by the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a narrative arc in which an outsider or skeptical figure witnesses the martyrdom and is converted or morally transformed; this provides a didactic closure that reinforces the drama's religious/message relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of studying obscure authors: novelty yields greater learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Of geniuses who remained obscure the essay says: 'from what is new to us we in general learn most' and that such authors may 'have more of [honey] for us than greater men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or learning creative writing and criticism, prioritize engagement with lesser-known 'obscure' geniuses for fresh stimulus and the highest potential for new insight rather than repeatedly reworking the well-known canonical texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of a literary 'genius' worth studying
rubrics_metrics.description: A genius is defined as one who 'has had a genuine gift for what is true and excellent, and is therefore capable of emitting a life-giving stimulus' — someone who prefers perfecting himself to seeking fame, and whose writings give an immediate contact with singular insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate writers for the presence of intrinsic moral/intellectual seriousness, the capacity to provoke thought in readers ('life-giving stimulus'), and honest craft (preference for being over seeming); these are the qualities that make study of an author particularly rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial virtue as evaluative criterion (perfection over reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Joubert is praised for caring 'far more about perfecting himself than about making himself a reputation' and for preferring 'being to seeming, knowing to showing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing a writer's merit, consider personal artistic virtues (integrity, seriousness, pursuit of perfection) alongside textual qualities; such virtues often correlate with enduring artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reading guidance for Joubert's fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary chapter of Joubert's fragments 'has some fancifulness and affectation in it; the reader should begin with the second.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When approaching Joubert's collected fragments, skip or de-emphasize the first chapter and begin reading at the second chapter for a clearer, less affected entry to his thought.
